abstract: |
  Response bias may refer to an observed tendency to respond "yes" or the location of a criterion on a latent evidence scale. The standard index, $c$, measures the second under an equal-variance Gaussian model. I evaluate PPB (Positive Predictive Bias), the sum of the hit and false alarm rates, as a measure of the first, paired with their difference, Youden's J. PPB is twice the yes rate examined by Macmillan and Creelman (1990). When both rates are between 0 and 1, PPB corresponds to criterion location under an equal-variance uniform model. Because it is linear in the rates, PPB, unlike $c$, is defined at rates of 0 or 1, is unbiased, averages exactly across observers, and expresses covariate effects in probability units. Exact calculations show that boundary corrections biased $c$ by up to 0.12 in the configurations tested. In simulations, the mean of individual $c$ values differed from $c$ at the mean rates by nearly half the latter’s magnitude. To properly quantify uncertainty when trials are few, I construct a conservative confidence interval with guaranteed binomial coverage. In eyewitness data, 62% of participants had a rate of 0 or 1 (Colloff et al., 2022); in three experiments with one trial per type, $c$ was undefined for every participant (or 0 under the $1/2N$ correction), while PPB revealed that showups raised identification probability, averaged across target-present and target-absent trials, by 5 to 19 percentage points relative to simultaneous showups (Colloff & Wixted, 2020).

keywords: [signal detection theory, response bias, ROC analysis, nonparametric statistics, Youden's J]

# Introduction

The criterion measure $c$ is the standard index of response bias in signal detection analyses.

Two problems recur when researchers seek to distinguish response bias (the tendency to favor one response) from classification accuracy. First, the criterion measure $c$ becomes undefined when either response rate equals 0 or 1, which is common when observers complete few trials or respond accurately. For example, participants in the eyewitness lineup study by Colloff et al. [-@colloff_active_2022] completed only four target-present (signal) and four target-absent (noise) lineup trials each. Since most eyewitness experiments test each witness once [@mickes_receiver_2012], $c$ often cannot be computed for individual witnesses at all.

The second problem is more conceptual. Researchers often describe $c$ as a measure of the tendency to respond "yes" or "no." Yet, more precisely, it locates the evidence value above which an observer responds "yes" on an unobserved evidence scale, referred to as the decision criterion. While these two readings do coincide at fixed $d'$ under the assumption of Gaussian distributions, they diverge when $d'$ varies or the distributions differ. Many applied researchers instead work directly with the two observed rates or simple functions of them [@rotello_when_2015]. A single summary of response propensity is useful for ranking observers, relating bias to other variables, or estimating covariate effects.

Positive Predictive Bias (PPB), defined as the true positive rate (TPR, or hit rate $H$) plus the false positive rate (FPR, or false alarm rate $F$), addresses both problems. It complements Youden's $J = \text{TPR} - \text{FPR}$ [@youden_index_1950; @peirce_numerical_1884] in the same way that $c$ complements $d'$. $J$ and PPB are perpendicular contrasts of the same two rates, summarizing accuracy and response bias, respectively.

@macmillan_response_1990 [p. 409] classify bias indexes according to both their assumed latent distributions and their target parameters. The decision criterion is the threshold on an observer’s internal evidence scale above which they respond "yes." Under the equal-variance uniform model, TPR + FPR is linearly related to this threshold’s position relative to the midpoint of the two evidence distributions. With equal numbers of signal and noise trials, $(H + F)/2$ is the proportion of "yes" responses, which Macmillan and Creelman call the yes rate [-@macmillan_response_1990, p. 406]. They investigate the yes rate against other bias indexes on key measurement properties: monotonic constant-bias (isobias) curves that behave sensibly at and below chance, range independence (parallel isobias curves on some coordinates), pooling across observers without distortion (aggregation), so that the index computed from a group's mean rates equals the mean of the individual indexes, and a known sampling distribution. The yes rate is the only index rated positively on all six pragmatic criteria in their Table 2 [-@macmillan_response_1990, p. 412]; $c$, by contrast, is rated marginal for aggregation, since pooling observers who differ in accuracy distorts the metric (Table 2, p. 412).

Macmillan and Creelman recommend pairing bias and sensitivity indexes from the same model [-@macmillan_response_1990, p. 411]. Their preference for normal and logistic models over uniform ones, based on ROC predictions, led them to favor $c$ alongside $d'$. When accuracy is measured by $J$, the same principle favors the yes rate. They regard criterion-location indexes, including the yes rate, as the best bias statistics (p. 412). Current calculation guides and software present $c$, $\beta$, and $B''$ [@stanislaw_calculation_1999]. The yes rate has received little further attention.

Exact unbiasedness under binomial sampling and exact aggregation are shared by fixed linear combinations of the two rates. PPB uses their sum, $H+F$, because it represents twice the probability of responding "yes" under equal presentation without assumptions about latent evidence distributions, and forms a perpendicular contrast to $J$. This paper revisits the yes rate through a theoretical and empirical evaluation of its interpretation, estimation, and practical advantages as a complement to $J$. PPB can also be computed without correction when either rate is 0 or 1. A covariate’s effect on PPB is expressed as a change in $H+F$, in probability units. I examine PPB's relation to criterion location, quantify the consequences of boundary corrections and aggregation in exact calculations and simulations, and construct confidence intervals for sparse counts. Eyewitness datasets illustrate estimation with few trials per observer, and two recognition-memory datasets assess whether PPB and $c$ remain stable across memory-strength manipulations.

# Definition and Properties

Consider an observer with rates $H$ and $F$, estimated from $n_s$ signal trials and $n_n$ noise trials. PPB is defined as

$$\text{PPB} = H + F$$ {#eq-ppb}

PPB is twice the yes rate of Macmillan and Creelman [-@macmillan_response_1990, p. 406]; doubling places balanced response propensity at 1 and simplifies @eq-inverse. Values above 1 indicate liberal responding, and values below 1 conservative responding, relative to equal presentation of the two trial types. PPB is distinct from positive predictive value, the proportion of positive responses that are correct. With signal probability $\pi$, the overall proportion of "yes" responses is $\pi H + (1 - \pi)F$, which equals PPB/2 when $\pi = 1/2$. The criterion interpretation below (@eq-crect) uses rates within each trial type and does not require $\pi = 1/2$ (Supplement §1.4). Response tendency has consequences apart from accuracy: liberal responding by an eyewitness means more identifications of innocent suspects [@wells_eyewitness_2003], conservative responding by a radiologist may miss cancers, and radiologists reading the same mammograms differ several-fold in false positive rate [@elmore_screening_2002].

Youden's $J = H - F$ measures accuracy in the observed rates, as $d'$ measures discriminability on the latent scale under equal-variance Gaussian signal detection theory (EVSDT). $J$ and PPB form a perpendicular pair of contrasts on the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) unit square (@fig-roc, Panel A):

$$H = \frac{J + \text{PPB}}{2}, \qquad F = \frac{\text{PPB} - J}{2}$$ {#eq-inverse}

Because both rates lie in $[0, 1]$, @eq-inverse implies the joint range $|J| \le \text{PPB} \le 2 - |J|$, a diamond in the $(J, \text{PPB})$ plane. PPB spans its full range, $[0, 2]$, only when $J = 0$; when $J = 0.87$, PPB must lie between 0.87 and 1.13. A raw PPB difference therefore represents a larger share of the available range in the more accurate group. These bounds concern attainable values at fixed observed $J$, not Macmillan and Creelman's range independence [-@macmillan_response_1990, pp. 409, 411]. Perpendicular contrasts are also not statistically independent: for fixed trial counts, the sampling covariance of PPB and $J$ is $\operatorname{Var}(\hat H) - \operatorname{Var}(\hat F)$ (Supplement §5).

By linearity, $\widehat{\text{PPB}}$ is exactly unbiased for PPB at every combination of $n_s$, $n_n$, $H$, and $F$, and independence between the two trial types gives

$$\operatorname{Var}(\widehat{\text{PPB}}) = \frac{H(1 - H)}{n_s} + \frac{F(1 - F)}{n_n}$$ {#eq-variance}

For observers with few trials, I construct a conservative interval by adding the lower bounds of the Clopper--Pearson intervals for $H$ and $F$ and, separately, their upper bounds, each at confidence level $1 - \alpha/2$ [@clopper_use_1934]; the sum covers PPB with probability at least $1 - \alpha$ under binomial sampling, boundary observations included. The plug-in normal-approximation interval can under-cover or collapse to zero width with sparse counts. A narrower adjusted interval, Agresti and Caffo's [-@agresti_simple_2000] interval for $H - (1 - F)$ shifted by one, has no coverage guarantee, so I examine its coverage by enumeration. Population means and paired condition differences need uncertainty across participants instead (Supplement §5).

Under EVSDT, $(d', c)$ are the corresponding contrasts of probit-transformed rates (zROC space):

$$d' = z(H) - z(F), \qquad -2c = z(H) + z(F)$$ {#eq-sdt}

Here $\Phi$ and $\phi$ are the standard-normal cumulative distribution and density functions, and $z = \Phi^{-1}$. With noise and signal evidence Gaussian with unit variance and means 0 and $d'$, $H = \Phi(d'/2 - c)$ and $F = \Phi(-d'/2 - c)$, so $c$ locates the criterion relative to the midpoint between the two means (Supplement §1.2). Because $\Phi$ is increasing, PPB decreases in $c$ at fixed $d'$:

$$\frac{\partial \text{PPB}}{\partial c} = -\left[\phi(d'/2 - c) + \phi(-d'/2 - c)\right] < 0$$ {#eq-monotone}

PPB and $c$ therefore rank observers consistently whenever $\Delta H$ and $\Delta F$ have the same sign: for any strictly increasing link $g$, $\Delta g(H) + \Delta g(F)$ then shares the sign of $\Delta H + \Delta F$, so every link-based criterion agrees with PPB. Divergent rankings require the rates to move in opposite directions, $|\Delta J| > |\Delta \text{PPB}|$, a necessary but not sufficient condition that is typical when groups differ in accuracy. Groups with the same PPB can differ in accuracy, as measured by $J$, and then receive different values of $c$ (see Group comparisons).

Interpreting PPB as criterion location, like interpreting $c$, invokes a model. Suppose that noise evidence is uniformly distributed on $[0, 1]$ and signal evidence on $[\delta, 1 + \delta]$. When the criterion $\theta$ lies within both distributions, $F = 1 - \theta$ and $H = 1 - \theta + \delta$, so $\delta = J$. Measured from the midpoint of the two distribution means, the criterion is

$$c_{\text{rect}} = \theta - \frac{1 + \delta}{2} = \frac{1 - \text{PPB}}{2}$$ {#eq-crect}

@eq-crect is Macmillan and Creelman's $k = 0.5[1 - (F + H)]$ [-@macmillan_response_1990, p. 406]. Their paired sensitivity parameter is $H - F = J$, which Snodgrass and Corwin [-@snodgrass_pragmatics_1988] call $P_r$. The criterion expression does not involve discriminability: observers who place the criterion at the same position relative to the midpoint have the same PPB at every $J$, in parallel with the independence of $c$ from $d'$ under EVSDT. The relation holds when the criterion lies in the distributions' overlap, endpoints included; outside it, the affine (linear plus a constant) formula need not recover criterion location, while PPB retains its yes-rate interpretation (Supplement §1.4). The uniform model implies a straight interior ROC segment of unit slope, with additional segments along the edges of the ROC square. Empirical ROC curves generally depart from the shape predicted by the uniform model. I use the model here to derive PPB’s relation to criterion location, without assuming that it describes the datasets analyzed below.

PPB’s relation to criterion location can also be expressed using the generalized linear model formulation of signal detection theory [@decarlo_signal_1998], where $d'$ is the difference of link-transformed rates and the criterion is their sum, up to scale. Replacing the probit with the identity link centered on balanced response propensity, $z(p) = p - \frac{1}{2}$, yields $J$ and $(1 - \text{PPB})/2$ (Supplement §1.4).

PPB differs from the other nonparametric bias indexes in aggregation, behavior at below-chance accuracy, and dependence on accuracy. The indexes $B''$ [@grier_nonparametric_1971] and $B''_D$ [@donaldson_measuring_1992] are built from products and ratios of the two rates and do not generally aggregate exactly (see Aggregation). Further, $B''$ must be reversed by hand for below-chance performance ($H < F$) [@grier_nonparametric_1971], whereas PPB remains continuous there and keeps its yes-rate interpretation. Snodgrass and Corwin [-@snodgrass_pragmatics_1988] pair $J$ with $B_r = F/(1 - J)$, the probability of responding "yes" from an uncertain evidence state under the same model as PPB; it is equivalent to Macmillan and Creelman's error ratio $k'$ [-@macmillan_response_1990, p. 406], and its denominator is zero at $H = 1$ and $F = 0$. $B_r$ normalizes criterion location by the width of the uncertain region, as $c'$ normalizes $c$ by $d'$, so for fixed $0 \le J < 1$ it spans $[0, 1]$. Curves of constant yes rate are parallel, whereas curves of constant error ratio radiate from a common point, so the two indexes can rank observers with different levels of accuracy differently.

Snodgrass and Corwin [-@snodgrass_pragmatics_1988] evaluate bias and discrimination indexes on the principle that a bias index should remain invariant under manipulations of discriminability, and a discrimination index under manipulations of bias. In a $2 \times 3$ within-subjects design crossing word imagery with three payoff matrices (different rewards and penalties for correct responses and errors), a valid bias index should track the payoff manipulation, remain stable across imagery conditions, and show a similar payoff effect in each imagery condition. The pair $(J, B_r)$ and the criterion indexes of the normal and logistic models pass; $\ln \beta$, $B''$, and $B'_H$ fail on the interaction. Snodgrass and Corwin did not test the yes rate as an index, although they report $H$ and $F$ separately.

Which index stays invariant depends on how observers set the criterion as discriminability changes, which an evidence model does not specify: they might keep its position relative to the midpoint or keep the probability of responding "yes" under equal presentation, and which rule they follow is an empirical question. Studies of recognition memory find that observers often keep a criterion fixed when item strength changes, at least within a test list [@stretch_difference_1998; @verde_memory_2007]. Under EVSDT, an observer who maintains $c = -0.5$ has $(H, F) = (0.84, 0.50)$ at $d' = 1$ and $(H, F) = (0.93, 0.31)$ at $d' = 2$. PPB consequently falls from 1.34 to 1.24 while $c$ remains constant. In the uniform model, holding criterion location fixed relative to the midpoint keeps PPB constant as $J$ changes. Holding the guess rate $B_r$ fixed gives a different result: with $B_r = 0.40$, PPB rises from 0.86 to 0.92 as $J$ increases from 0.3 to 0.6.

Under EVSDT the probit inverts the distribution function that generated the rates, so $c$ recovers criterion location; however it may not with non-Gaussian latent distributions (Supplement §1.3). In recognition memory studies, confidence-based zROC slopes are typically near 0.8, implying a signal standard deviation about 1.25 times that of the noise distribution [@ratcliff_testing_1992; @mickes_direct_2007]. A single operating point cannot estimate this ratio, so $c$ computed from one pair of rates assumes it equals 1. PPB’s interpretation as twice the probability of responding "yes" under equal presentation requires no assumptions about latent evidence distributions, whereas $c$’s criterion interpretation requires EVSDT.

# Methods

## Analysis design

The boundary-stability and follow-up analyses are exact calculations and the other original analyses are simulations; their reported trial counts are totals split equally between signal and noise trials. A separate interval analysis enumerates binomial outcomes at four, ten, and twenty trials per class, including unequal denominators, across a grid of operating points (pairs of hit and false alarm rates; Supplement §5). Two further simulations, of groups with similar PPB and different accuracy, are in Supplement §7. The supplement gives the derivations, and Supplement §9 gives the simulation settings.

Four analyses examine three practical properties of PPB: computability at rates of 0 or 1 without correction, covariate effects expressed as changes in $H+F$, and equality between mean individual PPB and PPB computed from the same mean rates.

The boundary-stability analysis used four configurations chosen so that boundary estimates would be common: $(H, F, n)$ = $(0.80, 0.05, 20)$, $(0.95, 0.20, 20)$, $(0.95, 0.05, 20)$, and $(0.95, 0.10, 40)$. For each, I computed the exact expected bias of PPB and of $c$ after either the log-linear correction [@hautus_corrections_1995] or the $1/2N$ correction [see @macmillan_detection_1985] by enumerating every binomial outcome.

The regression simulation assigned the same logit-scale bias coefficient ($\beta = 0.3$) to two accuracy groups and compared their estimated slopes (2,000 subjects per group, 40 trials per subject, one simulated data set per group; the slopes of $c$ use log-linearly corrected rates).

The aggregation simulation drew individual rates from beta distributions under three parameter settings. For PPB, $c$, $B''$, $B''_D$, and $B_r$, it compared the mean of 100 individual estimates with the estimate computed from the mean rates over 2,000 replications. Finally, an exact follow-up calculation examined the effects of applying corrections before aggregation and of excluding subjects whose estimated rates reached a boundary.

## Data

In addition to the simulations, I reanalyzed Experiment 1 from Colloff et al. [-@colloff_active_2022], a public eyewitness lineup dataset distributed in the pyWitness repository ([github.com/lmickes/pyWitness](https://github.com/lmickes/pyWitness); @mickes_pywitness_2024). The study included 220 participants, each of whom judged own-race lineups (faces from their own racial group) and other-race lineups (faces from another racial group). Each participant made eight decisions: four for target-present lineups and four for target-absent lineups. The present analysis pools across the interactive and static lineup conditions because that manipulation was crossed independently with the comparisons of interest.

The response in the primary analysis is choosing someone versus rejecting the lineup. Here, $H$ is the proportion of target-present trials on which any lineup member was chosen, whether the perpetrator or an innocent member (foil). $F$ is the proportion of target-absent trials on which any lineup member was chosen. Rejections are negative responses in both trial types. Here $J$ measures the separation between target-present and target-absent choosing rates. I computed PPB, $c$ (uncorrected and with each correction), $B''$, and $B_r$ for each participant overall and separately for their own-race and other-race lineups. The subject-level analysis pooled the race conditions, yielding four signal and four noise trials for each of 220 participants. The condition-level analysis separated own-race and other-race lineups, yielding two trials of each type in each of 440 participant-by-condition observations. The own-race contrast uses a t-based confidence interval for the mean within-participant difference, rather than treating trials as independent observations. Supplement §6 gives the response mapping and category counts.

I also reanalyzed Experiments 1 to 3 of Colloff and Wixted [-@colloff_why_2020], in which each participant made one target-present and one target-absent decision in a single identification condition. I compared the showup condition with the simultaneous-showup condition on participant-level PPB, $J$, and log-linear $c$, using Welch intervals. I omitted the standard-lineup condition of Experiment 3, because a positive response there is any face choice, so $J$ would not measure suspect identification (Supplement §8).

For Snodgrass and Corwin's test I used Experiments 1 and 2 of Layher et al. [-@layher_who_2020], with 1,000 trials per participant and cell, and the Measuring Memory Project [@starns_assessing_2019], with 100 per participant. In these reanalyses, memory strength was manipulated by varying the number of times each face or word was studied. I computed PPB and $J$ from raw rates and $c$ from log-linear corrected rates and tested each by two-way analysis of variance. I use Snodgrass and Corwin’s ANOVA criteria as a descriptive check and report differences between the strongest and weakest study conditions, with confidence intervals for each comparison.

# Results

## Boundary stability

A rate of 0 or 1 is a boundary rate. PPB is defined there, because it is a sum of two rates that may each lie anywhere in $[0, 1]$. The probit transformation for $c$ diverges at 0 and 1, so an observer with a boundary rate needs a correction before $c$ can be calculated. The standard log-linear [@hautus_corrections_1995] and $1/2N$ [see @macmillan_detection_1985] corrections give different estimates. In the four configurations, 44\% to 84\% of subjects produced a boundary estimate.

PPB remained unbiased in every configuration. Both corrections left $c$ nearly unbiased only in the configuration with $F = 1 - H$ ($H = 0.95$, $F = 0.05$), where the corrections to the two rates canceled.

In the other three configurations the log-linear correction biased $c$ by as much as 0.10, and the $1/2N$ correction by as much as 0.12 (@fig-advantages, Panel A). Relative to the population value of $c$, the corrections attenuated the population value of $c$ by 17\% to 31\% in configurations where $c$ differed from zero.

## Covariate effects in probability units

Applied researchers routinely relate detection and false positive rates to covariates, as in studies of how radiologists' interpretive performance and false positive rates vary with their characteristics [@miglioretti_radiologist_2007; @elmore_screening_2002] and of how partisanship and reflection shift response bias in judging news as true or false [@batailler_signal_2022]. When $H$ and $F$ are modeled separately, predicted PPB is predicted $H$ plus predicted $F$, so the covariate's effect on bias is the sum of its effects in the two models, in probability units, whatever link those models use.

The same additivity holds for $c$ on the $z$ scale. Unless the rate models use the probit link, however, each term must first be rescaled by $1/\phi(\Phi^{-1}(\cdot))$ before it corresponds to the rate models' effects (Supplement §4).

Effects in probability units and in criterion units answer different questions. A single coefficient on the logit scale can produce different probability-scale effects at different positions in ROC space. Criterion units are appropriate when the target is latent criterion location and EVSDT holds: under that model, a constant criterion shift changes $z(H)$ and $z(F)$ by a constant amount, and the probit removes probability-scale variation that reflects only the shape of the Gaussian distribution. When the question is how much a covariate changes the probability of a "yes" response, probability-scale variation is the target.

The same logit-scale bias coefficient produced a PPB slope of 0.040 among high-accuracy observers and 0.119 among moderate-accuracy observers, a threefold difference. The corresponding slopes for $c$, computed from log-linearly corrected rates, differed by a factor of 1.6 (@fig-advantages, Panel C). A constant logit-scale coefficient changes response probability by different amounts at different baseline rates, and these ratios show how that same change is expressed on the probability and probit scales. The ratios come from a single simulated data set; across 200 independent repetitions they averaged 2.7 for PPB and 1.4 for $c$ (Supplement §9). In addition, 794 of the 2,000 high-accuracy subjects required a correction before $c$ could be computed.

## Uncertainty with sparse counts

With few trials per observer, the usual normal-approximation interval for an individual's PPB is unreliable, so I compared three intervals on coverage and width: the normal-approximation interval, the guaranteed Clopper--Pearson sum interval, and the adjusted interval. The comparison used the four boundary-analysis configurations and a supplementary grid of configurations (Supplement §5).

In the four configurations, the normal-approximation interval’s nominal 95% coverage ranged from 85.76% to 98.62%. Across the grid it averaged 75.4% coverage, with a minimum of 7.7%.

The Clopper--Pearson sum interval guarantees at least nominal coverage under binomial sampling, but is wider. Across the grid its minimum coverage was 99.36%, which reflects its conservatism. At $H=0.80$, $F=0.05$, and ten trials per class, its expected width was 0.973, against 0.507 for the normal-approximation interval.

At that configuration the adjusted interval had expected width 0.597, without a coverage guarantee. Across the grid its coverage averaged 97.2% with a minimum of 91.5% and fell below 94% in 8.4% of configurations, and its mean expected width was 0.645, against 1.024 for the guaranteed interval.

Ordinary nonparametric resampling of an individual’s trials within each trial type leaves a boundary rate unchanged, yielding a zero-width percentile interval for that component. Participant-level bootstrap inference for population means or paired differences instead resamples whole participants and retains their paired measurements. A model-based bootstrap simulates responses from a fitted model, whose assumptions and estimates determine its behavior. Inverting an exact test for $H + F$ is possible and left for future work. The guaranteed interval supplies a conservative baseline; the adjusted interval offers a narrower option without the coverage guarantee.

## A design with one trial of each type

The most extreme boundary case is one decision of each type per participant, where every rate is 0 or 1. In Experiments 1 to 3 of Colloff and Wixted [-@colloff_why_2020], each participant made one target-present and one target-absent decision. The decision followed either a single face (showup) or that face among five similar faces, with the participant judging only the highlighted one (simultaneous showup).

Every participant therefore has $H_i$ and $F_i$ equal to 0 or 1, and $c$ is undefined for all of them. With one trial of each type, the $1/2N$ correction moves every rate to 1/2 and returns $c = 0$ for every participant, and excluding boundary participants leaves no data. PPB needs no correction.

Showups raised PPB relative to simultaneous showups by 0.102 (95% CI: 0.020 to 0.185; $N$ = 1,041), 0.107 (0.036 to 0.178; $N$ = 1,003), and 0.375 (0.307 to 0.444; $N$ = 1,087). In choosing probability these differences are 5.1, 5.4, and 18.8 percentage points. The intervals are Welch intervals on participant-level sums, which retain the dependence between a participant's two decisions.

The Experiment 3 difference is much larger than in Experiments 1 and 2. That experiment also changed task timing, instructions, and face selection, and the data do not identify which change, if any, produced the larger difference. No difference in $J$ was detected (estimated differences: 0.009, −0.022, and −0.014; every interval includes zero).

With one trial of each type, log-linear $c$ is an affine decreasing function of PPB and yields the same test statistics. Here $J$ is the separation of choosing rates in a binary response, not the confidence-based discriminability that Colloff and Wixted analyzed. Supplement §8 gives the condition means and the correction algebra.

## Aggregation

A group's bias can be summarized as the mean of the individual indexes or as the index computed from the group's mean rates. An index aggregates exactly when the two coincide; the aggregation discrepancy is the first minus the second. PPB aggregates exactly:

$$\overline{\text{PPB}} = \text{PPB}(\bar{H}, \bar{F})$$ {#eq-aggregation}

@eq-aggregation follows from the linearity of addition: averaging sums gives the sum of averages. Mean PPB is therefore twice the observers' mean probability of responding "yes" under equal presentation, regardless of heterogeneity in $d'$, and it summarizes response propensity.

Indexes that transform the rates nonlinearly generally do not aggregate exactly, because the average of a curved transformation is not the transformation of the average. For $c$, the probit is convex above 0.5 and concave below 0.5. Within a region of fixed curvature, Jensen's inequality fixes the direction of each rate's contribution to the discrepancy, and the two contributions can cancel. Mean $c$ summarizes criterion location under the Gaussian model, so it and $c$ at the mean rates are different quantities, and the discrepancy shows how much the choice between them matters.

Exact aggregation also holds when the same observer weights apply to both rates and to PPB. Pooling trials across observers weights each observer by trial count. Equal trial counts across observers within each trial type make pooled-trial rates equal unweighted observer means.

The aggregation discrepancy for PPB was zero to floating-point precision in every configuration. A negative discrepancy means the mean of the individual values is lower than the value at the mean rates. At high accuracy ($\mu_H = 0.90$, $\mu_F = 0.15$), the discrepancy for $c$ reached $-0.059$, nearly half the magnitude of $c$ at the mean rates (@fig-advantages, Panel B). The corresponding discrepancies were $-0.079$ for $B''$, $-0.052$ for $B''_D$, and $+0.033$ for $B_r$. Relative to the index at the mean rates, the discrepancy was 6\% for $B_r$ and 48\% for $c$. A common bias or common accuracy is sufficient for exact aggregation of $B_r$ but not necessary: zero covariance between individual $J$ and $B_r$ also suffices (Supplement §3).

Averaging corrected individual values retains their finite-sample bias even when all observers share the same population rates. At $H = 0.95$, $F = 0.20$, and $n = 20$, averaging log-linear-corrected individual values yielded bias of 0.10 in $c$ relative to its population value. Excluding subjects with boundary estimates before averaging increased the bias to 0.22 through selection. PPB required neither correction nor exclusion and remained unbiased when all observations were kept, hence its practical advantage is that it permits the retention of all observations.

## Group comparisons

Two groups can differ in bias by one index and not by another, because the indexes weight the same two rates differently. PPB adds $H$ and $F$ on the probability scale, whereas $c$ adds their probit transforms, and the transformation stretches the scale near 0 and 1. Groups with similar PPB can therefore differ in $c$ when their accuracy differs.

Consider Group A with $H = 0.95$ and $F = 0.08$ and Group B with $H = 0.65$ and $F = 0.40$. Their values of PPB are 1.03 and 1.05, but $J$ is 0.87 and 0.25 and $c$ is $-0.12$ and $-0.07$. PPB ranks Group B as the more liberal, and $c$ ranks Group A as the more liberal. From A to B, $H$ falls by 0.30 and $F$ rises by 0.32, so PPB rises by 0.02. On the probit scale the fall in $H$ outweighs the rise in $F$ because the transformation stretches the scale near 0.95. Matching both $H$ and $F$ would make every index agree.

The two answer different questions, one about the probability of saying "yes" and one about criterion location under the Gaussian model. Supplement §7 simulates this comparison with 100 subjects per group. A second simulation uses 200 subjects per group matched on PPB but differing in the shape of their latent distributions; the rejection rates of the other indexes follow the difference in $J$.

## Stability of bias across memory-strength conditions

Snodgrass and Corwin’s criteria require a bias index to respond to the intended bias manipulation, such as payoffs or instructions, without a detected effect of memory strength or an interaction between the two. Memory strength was manipulated by the number of study presentations. Statistics below are reported in the order PPB, then $c$.

PPB and $c$ met these criteria under payoffs and instructions. In Experiment 1 of Layher et al. [-@layher_who_2020], faces were studied once or five times and tested under three payoff schedules within subjects ($N = 39$). Payoffs affected both indexes, while memory-strength and interaction effects were not significant: payoff $F(2, 76) = 205.2$ and 166.9, strength $p = .63$ and .95, interaction $p = .20$ and .95. In the Measuring Memory Project [@starns_assessing_2019], words were studied one to three times and bias instructions varied between subjects ($N = 459$). Instructions affected both indexes, while memory-strength and interaction effects were not significant: instruction $F(2, 450) = 14.7$ and 13.6, strength $p = .55$ and .15, interaction $p = .20$ and .42.

Under the base-rate manipulation of Layher et al., every index failed, $c$, $J$ and $d'$ included. Raw $J$ also showed payoff and interaction effects in Layher Experiment 1, and in the Measuring Memory analysis it showed a strength effect but no instruction or interaction effect (Supplement §1.5).

I also estimated the memory-strength effect separately within each bias condition. The Layher Experiment 1 conservative-minus-liberal difference in PPB strength effects was 0.066, with a paired 95% interval of [$-0.020$, $0.152$]. In Measuring Memory, the conservative-instruction strength effect on PPB was 0.090, with interval [$0.026$, $0.155$]; the corresponding effect on $c$ was $-0.190$, with interval [$-0.316$, $-0.065$]. Some condition-specific confidence intervals therefore indicate departures from invariance despite the nonsignificant overall tests.

Neither dataset replicates Snodgrass and Corwin's design. Layher et al. used poorly discriminated faces ($d' \le 1.1$) and confounded strength with practice, the Measuring Memory Project induced bias by instruction between subjects, and neither manipulates word imagery.

## Boundary rates and aggregation in eyewitness data

I applied these measures to Experiment 1 of Colloff et al. [-@colloff_active_2022], where boundary rates were common. Each of 220 participants viewed four target-present and four target-absent lineups, two of each type in each of two conditions (own-race and other-race). A "yes" here is any lineup choice, so $H$ and $F$ are choosing rates.

At the subject level, 136 of 220 participants (62\%) produced at least one rate equal to 0 or 1 and so required a correction for $c$ (@tbl-empirical). At the condition level, with each participant in each condition counted as one observation, 89\% of observations required correction. PPB remained directly computable for every observation. The denominator of $B_r$ equaled zero ($H = 1$, $F = 0$) for 28 participants (13\%) and 146 of the 440 condition-level observations (33\%).

Among the 136 affected participants, estimates of $c$ under the log-linear and $1/2N$ corrections differed by as much as 0.14. The corrections also differed by as much as 0.15 among interior rates, because the log-linear method adjusts every rate, whereas the $1/2N$ method adjusts only boundary values.

Boundary estimates were concentrated among participants with the strongest separation between target-present and target-absent choosing rates. With only four trials of each type, rates near 0 or 1 often yield boundary estimates. Boundary prevalence increased across $J$ quartiles: 18\%, 46\%, 83\%, and 100\% (@tbl-quartiles).

For aggregation, the value of $c$ computed from mean corrected rates was $-0.1316$, whereas the mean of individual $c$ values was $-0.1418$. The resulting discrepancy was $-0.0102$. These are different criterion summaries, and the discrepancy was small in absolute units. PPB aggregated exactly under the common participant weights.

### Worked reporting example

Across 880 target-present trials there were 623 perpetrator choices, 95 foil choices, and 162 rejections; across 880 target-absent trials there were 261 foil choices and 619 rejections. Counting any choice as a "yes", $H = 718/880 = 0.8159$ and $F = 261/880 = 0.2966$, so $J = 0.5193$ and PPB $= 1.1125$. Because the trial types are equally frequent, PPB/2 $= 0.55625$ is the overall fraction of trials on which a witness chose. This statement is descriptive and needs no latent evidence model.

The point estimates indicated more choosing in own-race lineups (PPB$_{\text{own}} = 1.1341$, PPB$_{\text{other}} = 1.0909$; $c_{\text{own}} = -0.1297$, $c_{\text{other}} = -0.0879$). The paired own-minus-other PPB difference was 0.0432, with a 95% t-based confidence interval of [$-0.0348$, $0.1211$]. Dividing the difference and interval by two gives a choosing-probability difference of 0.0216, with interval [$-0.0174$, $0.0606$].

The point estimates agree in direction across PPB and corrected $c$, but the interval includes zero, so the choosing difference is imprecisely estimated. With two trials of each type per condition, log-linear $c$ is an affine decreasing function of PPB, so agreement in ordering the conditions follows algebraically. The estimate based on $c$ also depends on corrections for 89\% of the condition-level observations.

# Discussion

PPB summarizes response bias in probability units, remains computable without boundary corrections, and averages exactly across observers with common weights. Paired with Youden’s $J$, it revives Macmillan and Creelman’s yes rate.

In the eyewitness data, $c$ was undefined for 62% of participants without a correction. At 10 to 20 trials of each type, boundary corrections introduced bias of up to 0.12 in the tested configurations. In the high-accuracy aggregation simulation, the two group summaries of $c$, the mean of individual values and the value at the mean rates, differed by nearly half the latter’s magnitude. PPB required no correction, and its two summaries coincide.

PPB’s computational and aggregation properties follow from its linearity in $H$ and $F$. Its affine transform $(1-\text{PPB})/2$ gives the criterion contrast under the centered identity link. Pairing PPB with $J$ follows Macmillan and Creelman’s principle of deriving bias and sensitivity indexes from the same model [-@macmillan_response_1990, p. 411].

$H$ and $F$ describe responding on signal and noise trials. Each depends on both $J$ and PPB (@eq-inverse): at the same PPB, a group with higher $J$ has a higher $H$ and a lower $F$. PPB supplies a single response-propensity estimate for comparisons and covariate analyses. Testing $H$ and $F$ jointly can detect a difference in either component; it does not provide a single bias estimate. Questions about a particular rate, such as false identifications, are answered directly by that rate.

Hierarchical models account for participant and item variation [@rouder_introduction_2005; @morey_problematic_2008]. Models of radiologists’ performance already estimate hit and false alarm rates jointly [@miglioretti_radiologist_2007]. Summing fitted rates gives PPB in probability units. With common observer weights, PPB at the mean fitted rates equals the mean of individual fitted PPBs. Mean individual $c$ and $c$ at the mean fitted rates remain different estimands.

PPB's advantages matter most under four conditions. First, boundary rates are common when observers complete few trials or respond accurately: in eyewitness lineups; in diagnostic mammography, where radiologists each interpreted a median of eight cancers and observed rates reached 100% sensitivity and 0% false positives [@miglioretti_radiologist_2007]; and in truth-discernment tasks, where perfect accuracy leaves $d'$ undefined without an adjustment [@batailler_signal_2022].

Second, only group-level rates may exist, as when each witness is tested once [@mickes_receiver_2012]. Individual PPB cannot be computed when each witness completes only one trial type, but group PPB can estimate the population mean response sum if the witnesses who see target-present and target-absent lineups come from comparable populations. With unequal trial allocations, the weighting of the two rate pools also matters.

Third, rates may be modeled on covariates, as for radiologists [@miglioretti_radiologist_2007; @elmore_screening_2002] or for partisan bias in judging news [@batailler_signal_2022]. Covariate effects on PPB then add across the two rate models in probability units. PPB was introduced in such a setting: separate multilevel logistic models for $H$ and $F$ gave covariate-adjusted predicted rates, from which PPB and $J$ were computed with bootstrap intervals, across thousands of respondents judging social ties [@feltham_cognitive_2025].

Fourth, PPB's reading as a yes rate needs no assumptions about latent evidence distributions, which is useful in large, heterogeneous samples where EVSDT may be difficult to justify. The same reasoning applies to other classification tasks used to study group differences in judgment, such as the decision to shoot armed versus unarmed targets [@correll_across_2007], where accuracy and the tendency to respond "yes" are separate questions.

In practice, report the counts, $H$ and $F$, and pair PPB with $J$. PPB $= 1$ is a descriptive reference point for balanced responding under equal presentation. The response criterion appropriate to a task may depend on signal prevalence and error costs. Use the same participant weights in both rate means and in the mean PPB; the summaries then agree. Give uncertainty at the sampling unit appropriate to the question, using paired differences for repeated conditions.

For sparse individual counts, the Clopper--Pearson sum guarantees at least nominal coverage under the binomial model. The adjusted interval is a narrower approximate option that can under-cover in some of the evaluated configurations (Supplement §5). For covariate effects, model $H$ and $F$ separately and sum the predicted rates. Keep observers with boundary rates: excluding them biased $c$ by 0.22 in the follow-up calculation. When reporting $c$, name the correction and check that the conclusions survive the other one, because the two corrections disagree even for interior rates.

$c$ remains the better index when the question concerns latent criterion location and EVSDT has empirical support, as in psychophysical experiments where many trials yield interior rates; boundary corrections then matter less.

It is also the index to use when discriminability is manipulated and the researcher expects observers to hold a criterion fixed on the Gaussian evidence scale, because PPB then varies with $d'$ whenever $c$ differs from zero. The paradigm must justify that expectation. The open datasets did not decide it: the omnibus analyses detected no departures for $c$ under payoffs or instructions, but condition-specific intervals showed departures under conservative instructions.

Three limitations remain. First, the attainable range of PPB narrows as accuracy rises, $|J| \le \text{PPB} \le 2-|J|$, so comparisons should report $J$ alongside PPB. $B_r$ normalizes the uncertain region but is undefined at $H=1$, $F=0$. When individual $B_r$ values are defined, $B_r$ at equally weighted mean rates is their weighted average, with weights proportional to $1-J$ (Supplement §3).

Second, the empirical boundary illustrations concern choosing in two lineup datasets; they do not validate a suspect-identification criterion. The simulated configurations emphasize boundaries, and the recognition-memory datasets can only partially assess invariance.

Third, the guaranteed individual interval is wide, and the narrower adjusted interval has no guarantee (its coverage fell as low as 91.5% on the grid). Participant-level t-based confidence intervals are approximations, and dependence between participants or stimuli requires an analysis that preserves that structure.

Extensions include weighting for unequal presentation probabilities, multiclass and rating-scale data, and suspect-identification models for lineups. The difference $H - F$, Youden's $J$, has served as a distribution-free index of accuracy since @peirce_numerical_1884. PPB is its counterpart for bias.

# Data Availability {.unnumbered}

The Colloff et al. data are distributed in the [pyWitness published-data collection](https://github.com/lmickes/pyWitness/tree/main/data/published/2020_Colloff_Flowe_Smith_etal), which also holds the [Colloff and Wixted data](https://github.com/lmickes/pyWitness/tree/main/data/published/2020_Colloff_Wixted). The Layher et al. data are available at [OSF project 4k2hb](https://osf.io/4k2hb/), and the Measuring Memory Project data at [OSF project 92ahy](https://osf.io/92ahy/). I do not redistribute these datasets.

# Code Availability {.unnumbered}

The analysis code is available at [github.com/emfeltham/ppb-yes-rate-public](https://github.com/emfeltham/ppb-yes-rate-public), and an included "make" file regenerates every table, figure, and reported value. An R implementation of the PPB confidence intervals is included.
